title: Thessalonica
lead: A port city of Macedonia, founded about 315 BC by King Cassander of Macedon and named for his wife Thessalonike, a half-sister of Alexander the Great. Under Rome it became the capital of the province of Macedonia (128 BC) and a free city (41 BC), on the Via Egnatia. Paul founded a church there (Acts 17:1-10) and wrote it the two letters to the Thessalonians; Aristarchus and Secundus, his companions, came from there (Acts 20:4).

sections.b: Acts tells how Paul argued in the synagogue for three Sabbaths, won Jews, God-fearing Greeks and leading women, and was driven out after a riot in which Jason's house was stormed and Jason was brought before the city rulers, called politarchs, a title found in inscriptions from the city. The charge was that the missionaries said "that Jesus is another king" (Acts 17:7). Paul's letters show the church that remained: former idol worshipers who suffered from their neighbors and sent help to Paul (1 Thessalonians 1:9; 2:14; Philippians 4:16).
